newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu mulls next peace steps.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu mulls next peace steps.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a run-up to a U.S. visit this week, convened a special cabinet session on Monday to discuss further troop pullouts from the West Bank, his foreign minister said.

Netanyahu is to hold talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday. The cabinet session follows a summit late on Sunday between Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on the future of the Israeli-PLO peace process.

Foreign Minister David Levy, asked on Monday if ministers would discuss the depth of a further Israeli withdrawal in the West Bank planned for the first week of March, told army radio: "Today's cabinet discussion will be held on that exactly."

Levy, who called the Netanyahu-Arafat meeting "constructive", said the cabinet would debate whether the withdrawal would be made in areas currently under joint Israeli-PLO control, or if territory now under exclusive Israeli authority would also be handed over to Palestinian self-rule.

In a peace breakthrough in January, Israel handed 80 percent of the West Bank town of Hebron to PLO rule, ending months of rancourous debate both with the Palestinians and within Netanyahu's right-religious cabinet.
Arafat arrived in Hebron on Monday to spend the last day of the Moslem feast of Eid al-Fitr in the West Bank.
His two-day visit could coincide with the release by Israel of 25 Palestinian women prisoners. Officials from both sides said they would be freed either on Monday or Tuesday.

Prior to the Hebron pullout -- agreed with Israel's previous Labour government but suspended after Islamic suicide bombings early last year -- Arabs had voiced fears that the hawkish Netanyahu, elected last May, might bring peace moves to a halt.
Netanyahu said on Sunday he and Arafat had agreed to start detailed talks on future peace steps outlined in the Hebron pact.

"We agreed on a mechanism to resolve these issues and advance them," he said, adding that Israeli-Palestinian committees would begin talks next Sunday, with a committee on economics meeting before that.
By March 7 Israel is to start a three-stage troop withdrawal from rural areas it still occupies in the West Bank, a process to be completed by mid-1998.

Levy said the cabinet would decide on the additional pullout solely on the basis of security considerations. He reiterated Israel's insistence that it alone will determine the nature and depth of the pullbacks. The PLO insists they must be negotiated.

Arafat has complained of delays on other issues in the Hebron deal, including the operation of Palestinian sea and air ports, the release of Palestinian prisoners and "free passage" between Gaza and the West Bank.

"A month after the Hebron protocol was signed, many things should have been implemented, including the release of women (prisoners), but until now nothing has been implemented," Arafat's aide Nabil Abu Rdeinah told Reuters on Monday.
Arafat was upbeat after the Sunday summit.
"We had a very important meeting...We discussed the details of the problems we are facing, especially the points which have to be implemented after the Hebron agreement," Arafat said.
U.S. officials have expressed hopes that agreement on Hebron could pave the way for resumption of talks with Syria.
The Syrian track, seen as the cornerstone to an overall Middle East peace deal, has long been stalled over the strategic Golan Heights, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.
